respStmt.resp: traduction anglaise depuis le grec (zoo46/3g), verification humaine requise

sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise originale produite avec l'assistance d'un modele de langage (Claude, Anthropic), a partir du texte grec de zoo46/3g.xml (Pseudo-Dioscoride, Alexipharmaca), deja present dans le corpus Zoomathia. Traduction generee par IA, non relue par un specialiste : a verifier avant tout usage scientifique cite. Couvre les 32 substances traitees (signes cliniques puis traitement, dans l'ordre du temoin grec) ; le prooimion methodologique initial et les deux chapitres generaux de conclusion (sur les remedes pouvant aussi nuire, et sur ce qui est naturellement proche de nous) n'ont pas ete traduits, a la demande de l'utilisateur. Structure aplatie en chapitres continus depuis le decoupage interne, tres irregulier, du temoin grec source.

div.head: On cantharides (blister beetles)
div.p: In those who have taken cantharides, very grave signs follow: nearly everything from the mouth to the bladder seems to them to be gnawed; and in taste something like pitch or cedar-resin arises. The right hypochondrium becomes inflamed, and they pass urine with difficulty; often they void blood through the urine. In the bowels they pass matter resembling that of dysentery; they fall into faintness, sickness of stomach, and dizziness; and in the end their reason wanders. Before any such symptom follows, one must force them to vomit, giving them oil or one of the other things already mentioned, and after most of it has been brought up by vomiting, one should also inject through a clyster a broth of gruel, or rice, or spelt, or barley-water, or a decoction of mallow, or of flaxseed, or of fenugreek, or of the roots of marshmallow, which the Romans call ‘hibiscus.’ One should also give them soda with honey-water, to bring down and rinse out what still clings to the stomach and intestines; and if this does not suffice, one must purge them further, injecting honey-water with soda, and giving wine or sweet wine in which pine-nuts and cucumber-seed have been crushed, or milk, or honey-water, or goose-fat melted in sweet wine. The inflamed parts should be poulticed with barley-meal boiled in honey-water. At first, poultices thus applied do harm, because the heat generated holds what is given fast, fixing it upon the affected vital parts; but once some time has passed, they benefit the most severe inflammations, soothing and easing the pains. At this stage it is also fitting, after first anointing the body with a warming oil, to bathe them, setting them in a tub. For each, the cure works by drawing out through the surface, onto the body, what is harmful within; and in general one must stir the excretions in every way, so that the condition may not settle into a fixed and lasting state. One should also give them the meat of fowl, lamb, suckling pig, and kid, fatty and very tender, boiled with flaxseed, for these loosen the bowels and blunt what is sharp; and sweet wine in quantity.

Also helpful for them is the bark of frankincense, and the earth called ‘star-earth,’ four portions of each taken with sweet wine; pennyroyal rubbed with water; iris-oil or rose-oil with a decoction of rue; and the tender green shoots of the vine, ground fine with sweet wine. Most effective of all are the antidotes, drunk with honey-water in the amount of four portions.

div.head: On the pine-caterpillar
div.p: In those who have taken the pine-processionary caterpillar, pain about the mouth and palate follows at once; a severe inflammation of the tongue, the stomach, and the belly; a severe pain of the intestines, together with a sensation as though the inward parts were being gnawed; a burning over the whole body, and sickness. These should be helped in the same way as those who have drunk cantharides; but as a special measure for them we shall use, in place of plain oil or iris-oil, quince-oil, prepared from quinces and oil.

div.head: On the buprestis (a toxic beetle)
div.p: In those who have drunk the buprestis, there seems at first tasting to be something like foul-smelling soda; there follows a violent pain of the stomach and belly, and a swelling of the stomach and belly resembling that of the dropsical; and the surface of the whole body becomes stretched taut; the urine is suppressed. What helps those who have drunk cantharides helps them too; but as a special measure, once they have been purged by vomiting and by clyster, they are helped by taking dried figs, and a decoction of these with wine; and once the acute danger is past, they are helped by eating Theban dates, or by drinking them ground fine with wine-and-honey or milk, or by eating every kind of pear, and drinking woman’s milk.

div.head: On the salamander
div.p: In those who have taken the salamander, an inflammation of the tongue follows, together with confusion of mind, and trembling with a certain numbness or shivering and faintness; some parts of the body take on a livid, circular discoloration, so that often, if the poison persists, they putrefy and slough away. In their case, having done everything that is done for cantharides, we apply as a more particular remedy pine-resin, or galbanum with honey in place of a linctus, and a decoction of ground-pine, together with crushed pine-nuts, or nettle-leaves boiled with barley-groats and oil. Also helpful for them are the eggs of the sea-turtle or the land-tortoise, however they may be, boiled; and a broth of frogs, boiled together with the root of eryngo.

div.head: On the ephemeron (also called colchicum)
div.p: In those who have taken the ephemeron, which some call colchicum, or the wild bulb, an itching over the whole body follows, as though irritated by squill or nettle; the inward parts feel gnawed; there is a burning of the stomach with considerable heaviness; and as the affliction gains strength, bloody matter mixed with shreds is passed in the bowels. These should be helped, as those who have drunk salamander, by vomiting and by clysters; and before the drug takes full hold, one should give them a decoction of oak-leaves, or of acorns, or of pomegranate rind; or they should drink wild thyme with milk, or the juice of knotgrass, or of vine-shoots, or of bramble, or the pith of the tender fennel-giant, or myrtle with wine — the myrtle-berries themselves, crushed fine and steeped in water, are also helpful, the liquid from them being taken. The middle membrane of Sardian acorns, taken raw with one of the aforesaid juices, works likewise; oregano drunk with lye also helps; and those who drink warm ass’s or cow’s milk and hold it in the mouth are helped most precisely of all — so that those who can obtain this need no other remedy.

div.head: On doryknion (also called mad nightshade)
div.p: When doryknion is drunk — which some have called ‘mad nightshade’ — there follows a taste in the mouth as of milk, together with continual hiccoughing, moistness of the tongue, and a sudden bringing-up of blood; in the bowels they pass mucous matter, as in dysentery. Before any of this follows, they are helped by the same things as those already named: vomiting, the clyster, and whatever can expel the drug that has been drunk. As a special remedy for them, honey-water helps, or ass’s or goat’s milk, and warm sweet wine drunk with anise, and bitter almonds, and boiled fowl-breasts; and all shellfish, eaten raw or roasted, and crayfish, and lobsters, and the broth made from them, drunk.

div.head: On aconite
div.p: Aconite, as soon as it is drunk, sweetens the tongue with a certain astringency, and from this sweetness brings on dizziness, especially on standing up, and a moistness of the eyes, together with a heaviness of the chest and hypochondrium, and much passing of wind. In these cases the drug must be brought up by vomiting, or the bowels relieved by a clyster; we shall use as a preliminary draught oregano, or rue, or horehound, or a decoction of wormwood with wormwood-wine, or rocket, or southernwood, or spurge-olive, or ground-pine. Also fitting for them is one dram-weight of balsam-sap with honey and milk, together with castoreum, pepper, and rue in equal weight with wine; and rennet of kid, hare, or fawn with vinegar; and iron-slag, or iron itself, or gold, or silver, red-hot and quenched in wine, the liquid being taken; lye with wine; and the broth of boiled fowl or of fatty beef, taken with wine. Ground-pine is also said to be especially fitting for these cases.

div.head: On the honey of Heraclea
div.p: Those who eat or drink the honey produced at Heraclea on the Black Sea suffer likewise; for them the same remedies are fitting as for aconite. They are easily helped, benefiting especially from wine-and-honey, drunk continually, with rue-leaves mixed into it.

div.head: On coriander
div.p: Coriander cannot go unnoticed, because of its smell; drunk, it thickens the voice and brings on a madness resembling that of drunkenness — they speak, indeed, with shameful language — and the smell of the coriander shows through over their whole body. They are helped, once purged by vomiting through iris-oil, as said before, by unmixed wine drunk with wormwood, taken by itself; or by eggs beaten together and diluted with brine, sipped down; brine itself, drunk; and a salty broth from fowl or goose; or sweet broth taken with lye.

div.head: On psyllium (fleawort)
div.p: The plant called psyllium, when drunk, also brings on a chill over the whole body, and numbness, with faintness and distress. All that helps those who have drunk coriander helps this too.

div.head: On hemlock
div.p: Hemlock, when drunk, brings on dimness and a mist, so that one cannot see even a little, together with hiccoughing and wandering of the mind, and a chilling of the extremities; in the end, convulsed, they choke, the breath in the windpipe coming to a stop. At first, as with the others, we shall bring it up by vomiting; then, using a purge, we shall expel what has slipped down into the intestines; and then, as the greatest remedy, we come to the drinking of unmixed wine, giving it at intervals, in between which it also helps to give ass’s milk to drink, or wormwood with pepper, wine, and castoreum; rue and mint with wine; cardamom, or storax, or pepper with nettle-seed and wine; or bay-leaves; likewise silphium-sap with oil or with sweet wine; and much sweet wine drunk by itself is sufficiently fitting.

div.head: On the yew (called smilax)
div.p: The plant called smilax — by some, thymion, and among the Romans, taxus — when drunk brings on a chill over the whole body, choking, and swift death. What helps those who have drunk hemlock helps these as well.

div.head: On the sap of the carpasum-tree
div.p: The sap of the carpasum-tree, when drunk, brings on stupor and swift choking; these too are helped by the same things as those who have drunk hemlock.

div.head: On the sardonian herb
div.p: The herb called sardonian, a kind of crowfoot, when drunk or eaten, brings on wandering of the mind and convulsions with a contraction of the lips, so that it gives the appearance of laughter — from which condition ‘sardonic laughter’ has become an unflattering expression in common speech. In their case, especially after vomiting, much honey-water is fitting, given generously, and milk; a fomentation and anointing of the whole body with warming remedies, and a bath in hot water-and-oil. After the bath they must be anointed thoroughly and rubbed down. In general, the whole treatment should be conducted as for convulsion.

div.head: On henbane
div.p: Henbane, drunk or eaten, brings on a derangement resembling that of the drunk; it is easily cured, being helped by much honey-water given to drink, and especially by ass’s milk — failing that, goat’s or cow’s milk — or by a decoction of dried figs. Pine-nuts also help them, and cucumber-seed taken with sweet wine; salty wine with fresh pig-fat and sweet wine with water is fitting, and nettle-seed likewise, or soda with water; chicory too is fitting, and mustard, and cress, and radish, and onions, and garlic, each of these taken with wine. One must make them keep still, so that, having drunk the wine, they may digest it.

div.head: On the mandrake
div.p: When mandrake is drunk, a torpor follows at once, and faintness, and a heavy stupor no different from the affliction called lethargy. Before any of this occurs, vomiting is fitting, and honey-water, and after this soda and wormwood taken with sweet wine or wine sweetened; a fomentation of the head with rose-oil and vinegar; and the rousing and stirring of the body. So too the use of things smelled — pennyroyal, pepper, mustard, castoreum, and rue rubbed in vinegar; liquid pitch; and burnt, extinguished lamp-wicks. If they are hard to rouse, sneeze-inducing remedies should also be applied, and the other common remedies used in these cases as well.

div.head: On the sap of the poppy
div.p: When the sap of the poppy is drunk, a heavy stupor follows, together with chilling and an intense itching, so that often, as the drug takes stronger hold, so great an itching arises that they are roused by it; and the smell of the drug is given off over the whole body. They are helped, after vomiting up the oil, by being purged with a sharp clyster, and by drinking oxymel with salt, or honey with warm rose-oil; and much unmixed wine with wormwood or cinnamon; or warm vinegar by itself; soda with water; oregano with lye; the seed of wild rue with pepper, wine, and all-heal; pepper with castoreum and oxymel, or with savory or oregano and wine. One must also rouse them with the things called ‘things smelled,’ and set them in a warm bath, and foment them, because of the itching that follows. It will also benefit them, after the bath, to take fatty broths with wine or sweet wine, and marrow drunk with oil.

div.head: On the horned poppy
div.p: The plant called horned poppy, when eaten or drunk, brings on the same symptoms as the sap of the poppy, and falls under the same remedies.

div.head: On the pharikon
div.p: The substance called pharikon has, in taste, altogether the character of wild spikenard; drunk, it brings on paralysis together with derangement and convulsion. After making them vomit, one must give them wormwood-wine to drink, with cinnamon, or myrrh, or Cilician nard, which some have called ‘neris’; or two dram-weights of spikenard, or two obols of myrrh, mixed with sweet wine; and iris and saffron-flower with wine. Their heads should be shaved and poulticed with barley-meal mixed with ground rue and vinegar.

div.head: On toxicon (arrow-poison)
div.p: Toxicon seems to have taken its name from the fact that the arrows of foreign peoples are smeared with it. In those who have drunk it, there follows an inflammation of the lips and tongue, and an uncontrollable madness assailed by varied hallucinations, so that for this reason too such cases are hard to treat, and it is rare for any who have drunk it to be saved. One must nonetheless restrain them by force with bonds, and compel them to drink sweet wine with rose-oil and to vomit it up; the seed of turnip, drunk with wine; and, as a particular remedy for them, the root of cinquefoil, and the blood of a he-goat or she-goat, taken in like manner; the bark of oak, or of Valonia oak, or of holm-oak, ground fine with milk; quinces eaten, ground fine; or drunk with pennyroyal and water; cardamom, and the fruit of the balsam-tree with wine. And if any escape the danger of it, they remain bedridden for a long time, and even once risen, spend the rest of their days in a state of dread.

div.head: On ixia (also called oulophonon, ‘wool-killer’)
div.p: Ixia, also called oulophonon, when drunk, has something of the smell and taste of basil. It brings on a severe inflammation of the tongue and derangement; it checks all the excretions; it brings on rumblings and noises with faintness, without anything being passed. They are helped, once the greater part has been vomited up, or once the bowels have been loosened, by drinking a steeping of wormwood with much wine or with oxymel; the seed of wild rue, or the root of silphium; likewise a decoction of horse-mint with one of the aforesaid, or with milk, or with terebinth resin, or with nard, or castoreum, or silphium, an obol of each; the nuts of the royal walnut are also fitting, with wine, together with resin and castoreum and rue, one portion of each; likewise two obols of spurge-olive or of deadly carrot with honey-water, and warm vinegar drunk.

div.head: On white lead (psimythion)
div.p: White lead cannot go unnoticed, because of its color; taken deliberately, it whitens the palate, the gums, the tongue, and the spaces between the teeth. It brings on hiccoughing and coughing, dryness of the tongue, and a chilling of the extremities, together with derangement and difficulty of movement. For these, honey-water is fitting, or a decoction of figs or of mallow, or warm milk, or sesame ground fine with wine, or lye of vine-cuttings, or marjoram-oil, or iris-oil; peach-stones with a decoction of barley-groats; the eggs of doves with frankincense or a decoction of barley; or the gum of plums, or the sap found in the bark of the elm, with tepid water. Also fitting for them, drunk, is the juice of deadly carrot, or three obols of scammony-sap.

div.head: On mushrooms
div.p: Of mushrooms, some cause harm by their kind, others by their quantity; all bring on a choking resembling strangulation. These must be helped at once by the common remedy, forcing them to vomit with oil; they benefit remarkably from drinking lye made from vine-cuttings, or from wild-pear wood, with vinegar-and-water and salt or soda; wild pears, or their leaves, boiled together with the mushrooms, remove their choking effect, and eaten, they benefit. Hen’s eggs drunk with vinegar-and-water, with one dram-weight of aristolochia, also help them, or wormwood with wine; honey eaten and drunk with water; balm with soda; the root and fruit of all-heal with wine; the burnt lees of wine with water; verdigris with vinegar; and radish, or mustard, or cress, eaten.

div.head: On gypsum
div.p: Gypsum too brings on choking, once it has hardened like stone. For this reason the remedies given against mushrooms are fitting here also, and among these, a decoction of mallow, which should be taken in place of oil; for being oily, and causing slipperiness when vomited up, it prevents the body from being scraped raw — which is what hardened gypsum does. Oil with honey-water or a decoction of figs is also fitting; lye of fig-wood or of vine-cuttings, drunk with much wine; oregano or thyme with lye, or vinegar, or sweet wine. These patients should be purged below with the decoction of mallow.

div.head: On bull’s blood
div.p: Freshly slaughtered bull’s blood, when drunk, brings on difficulty of breathing and choking, blocking the passages about the tonsils and the gullet, together with severe convulsion. In such cases the tongue is found to be red, the teeth stained, and clots between them. In these cases we avoid inducing vomiting, since the clots would only be wedged more firmly in the stomach by being drawn upward; instead one should give whatever can dissolve the clotting of the blood and move the bowels — unripe figs, full of their sap, with oxymel; soda by itself also helps; every kind of rennet with vinegar, and the root or sap of silphium; likewise cabbage-seed, lye of fig-wood, and fleabane-leaves with pepper, and bramble-juice with vinegar. The bowels must be moved. In those who recover, it is usual for foul-smelling, flowing matter to be passed through the rectum. The stomach and belly should also be poulticed with barley-meal and honey-water.

div.head: On curdled milk
div.p: In those who have taken a great quantity of curdled milk at once, severe choking arises, because it clots. To help them, one must administer, as an antidote, rennet with vinegar, forcing them to drink it repeatedly; dried calamint-leaves, or the juice likewise; the root or sap of silphium with oxymel; thyme with wine; and fuller’s lye. Nothing salty should be given, for it makes the milk clot and curdle all the more. Nor should these patients be made to vomit, for the clotted mass, lodging in the narrow passage of the stomach, would cause choking.

div.head: On litharge
div.p: Litharge, when drunk, brings on a heaviness of the stomach, belly, and intestines, with intense griping; sometimes, because of its weight, it even wounds the intestines; it suppresses the urine; the body swells, and takes on a leaden, unsightly hue. For these, after vomiting, it is fitting to drink with wine: the seed of wild clary, an ounce of myrrh, or wormwood, hyssop, celery-seed, or pepper, or henna-flower with wine; and the dried droppings of wild doves with spikenard or wine.

div.head: On mercury (quicksilver)
div.p: Quicksilver, when drunk, brings on the same effects as litharge, and in these cases the same remedies should be used. Much milk drunk seems to benefit them; these too should vomit.

div.head: On lime, realgar, and arsenic
div.p: Lime, realgar, and arsenic, when drunk, bring on the same pains of the belly and intestines, with a violent gnawing sensation. Hence one must administer everything that, by its blending quality, can be soothing and can render the passage through the bowels slippery — such as the juice of marshmallow and of mallow, which is exceedingly slippery. A decoction of flaxseed, or of spelt, or of rice should also be given; and much milk with honey-water, and rich, wholesome broths.

div.head: On the sea-hare
div.p: When the sea-hare is drunk, there follows at first a taste like foul-smelling fish; as time passes, the belly aches and the urine is suppressed; and if it is ever passed, it appears purple in color; there is an aversion and loathing toward all fish; and they sweat with a foul odor. Bilious vomiting also follows, sometimes mixed with blood. To these one should give ass’s milk, or sweet milk continually, and a decoction of the root and leaves of mallow, or the root of cyclamen ground fine with wine; or one portion of black hellebore or of scammony-sap with honey-water; pomegranate seeds, or ground cedar-resin with wine. Goose’s blood, drunk warm, also helps. Those who cannot yet take fish should eat only boiled river-crabs, and, drinking wine mixed with water along with them, they digest it and are helped; and it is a sign of their recovery when they begin to be able to take fish again.

div.head: On the toad
div.p: The toad, or marsh-frog, when taken, brings on swellings of the body together with an intense pallor, so that one seems to resemble boxwood; difficulty of breathing follows, and the mouth smells foul; hiccoughing follows them, and sometimes an involuntary emission of seed. They are readily helped, after vomiting, by taking much unmixed wine, and two portions of reed-root, or the same amount of galingale. One must also compel them to walk about vigorously and to run, because of the numbness that is in them, and to bathe every day.

div.head: On leeches
div.p: Leeches that are swallowed along with water and attach themselves to the throat or to the mouth of the stomach, gnawing at the parts and producing a sensation like sucking — which is itself a sign that leeches have been swallowed — are expelled by drinking down brine, and Cyrenaic sap, or the leaves of silphium or of beet, drunk with vinegar, or snow with vinegar-and-water. One should also gargle with soda and water, and with vitriol dissolved in vinegar. For those that have attached to the windpipe, set the patient in a hot bath and give him cold water to hold in his mouth, and they will come out.
